title: Melania Trump seeks ‘solitude’ in new docuseries | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Melania Trump’s streaming docuseries, released by Amazon on Friday, reveals an introverted first lady who shares new insight into her marriage and priorities.

The pair of episodes — which complementthe eponymous documentarythat hit theaters earlier this year — were shot in January 2025 as she was preparing for her husband’s second inauguration and her first major trip, to a pair of natural disaster-ravaged sites.

But the scenes, now nearly two years old, offer a time capsule of what is now a bygone American era — lacking any context of the tumult and transformation of President Donald Trump’s second term or any information about how his wife has spent that time.

In the 10 months since the premier of the “MELANIA” documentary, the president went to war with Iran, the first lady brokered a temporary localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, and the nation delivered the MAGA movement a stunning rebuke in the midterm elections. None of that is covered in the new release.

While Melania Trump is shown in the series conferring with designer Tham Kannalikham over plans to “preserve” and “restore” and “build new stuff” at the White House, there is no mention of the president’s plans to tear down the East Wing, thehome to first ladies for decadesthat was suddenly razed last year. Nor does Melania Trump share her thoughts on her husband’s sprawling ballroom project — a topic on which she has remained silent.

Melania Trump does shed some light on why she keeps such a tight inner circle. “I’m not shy. I’m very selective,” she says.

“In this world, especially in politics, it’s very hard to trust people, and it’s a mean world. It’s very mean, and everybody has an agenda, and sometimes not pleasant.”

Melania Trump, who has spent most of the last two years in Palm Beach or New York, repeatedly says she craves “solitude.”

“For me, it’s very important I get enough sleep, also solitude, and be in peace and quiet. I don’t need to be all the time with people. I’m very happy in my own company,” she says when asked how she preserves her mental health.

The series then cuts to video of her walking the Mar-a-Lago grounds in a white hoodie, jeans and flat sandals (a rarity for the oft-stilettoed first lady).

“The spa brings me calmness, recentering my spirit, body, and mind,” she says in a voiceover, adding, “Women should honor their own natural beauty, which evolves as we age, all authentic, never alteration.”

And Melania Trump, her husband’s closest adviser, provides a rare window into that relationship.

“I tell him the truth. I feel that sometimes there are too many people around him that — they are yes people, and that’s not healthy,” she says.

Solitude, she notes, is “very important” for her marriage, too. “You need to let that person be who they are, and enjoy what they do, and not to be that they are overwhelmed with you and nagging all the time,” she says.

Donald Trump often tells a story on the campaign trail about how his wife doesn’t think it’s presidential when he dances to the “YMCA” on stage. Now we hear her side: “Sometimes, you know, the situations were like, ‘I don’t think it’s the good day to dance.’”

To the extent she gets political in the series, Melania Trump laments cancel culture, describing an incident where she had trouble doing business with banks after leaving the White House in 2021, and a separate situation where university board members canceled plans to work with her on a foster care initiative.

“When the board members start hearing that I’m involved, they cancel me. It’s a pity, because who suffered? The children suffered from foster communities. I knew that it was all political because — because of my last name,” she says.

In both “MELANIA” the documentary and “MELANIA: The Series,” director Brett Ratner emerges from his own fall from grace amid accusations of sexual misconduct (he has denied any wrongdoing), casting himself in a supporting role as he asks the president and first lady questions.

Amazon paid $40 million for the rights to the documentary and committed another $35 million for marketing — eye-poppingly high sums for a documentary. The Hollywood Reporter called it the “most expensive” such film in history at the time.

And as in the full-length documentary, there’s an emphasis on fashion in the series — including a scene where Melania Trump selects a one-of-a-kind vintage Harry Winston brooch to pair with her inaugural gown.

She also fashions herself a businesswoman, receiving a presentation on blockchain and AI as she explains that “emerging technology provides benefits for my entire fan base.”

She briefly touches on her hopes to expand her “Be Best” platform, suggesting she wants to “help children and families” and pointing to social media as one potential arena. But the new episodes are devoid of any specifics, including her support for the “TAKE IT DOWN Act” and her efforts to support youth aging out of the foster care system.

Though Trump famouslyquestioned, “Who gives a fuck about Christmas?” she makes clear that “managing the White House” and related events — the Easter Egg Roll, holiday decor and state dinners — are a key part of the role of a first lady. She spends time with event planner David Monn, who expresses hope that she will soon “have her own set” of official White House china.

“Today, meaningful impact is driven by action, and under my leadership, the East Wing will be defined by results, purpose, and lasting influence,” Melania Trump says over video of her working at a computer in her softly-lit, Mar-a-Lago office where a stack of glossy books on famous fashion designers — Dior, Chanel — sits atop a desk.
